overview.text: Escherichia coli (E. coli) is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium commonly found in the lower intestine of warm-blooded animals. Most strains do not cause illness, but certain strains have traits that let them cause disease, including diarrhea; Shiga toxin-producing strains can sometimes lead to serious kidney complications. E. coli is also important in science and biotechnology: researchers can manipulate it readily, grow it quickly and inexpensively, and use its well-studied genetics and available laboratory tools to produce recombinant proteins. Its distinguishing significance is this contrast: the same bacterial species includes ordinary gut inhabitants, disease-causing strains, and laboratory strains useful for research and production.

key_facts.text: E. coli is a Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium.
It commonly lives in the gastrointestinal tract, and most strains do not cause illness.
Disease-causing strains differ in their virulence traits; Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, particularly some O157 strains, can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome, which can damage the kidneys.
Certain extraintestinal pathogenic strains cause urinary tract infections; CDC reports that E. coli causes 80–90% of UTIs.
E. coli is widely used to produce recombinant proteins because it is relatively easy to manipulate and grow, and researchers have many compatible laboratory tools and strains.
